meta.title: AI adoption review checklist for Singapore hospitals
meta.description: Questions administrators and nurse leaders can ask when a vendor proposes an AI product: purpose, HSA status, patient data, security and operations.
meta.lead: Use this when you receive a specific proposal. Tick each item when you have a written answer. The items are the author’s list; the two checklists and the facts page give the sections of the documents behind many of them.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
items: The job the tool will do is described in one sentence and agreed by the department that will use it.
Who will use it, and who will be affected by its output, is listed (including nurses and front-desk staff).
The hospital’s AI governance platform, or whoever fills that role, has been asked to assess and approve the tool before purchase.

sections.heading: Regulatory status
items: The vendor states in writing whether it treats the product as a medical device in Singapore and why, based on its intended use.
If it is a medical device, the risk class and the HSA registration details are written down, and you have checked that your planned use matches the intended use.
The vendor explains how model updates are handled, including whether it uses HSA’s change notification and its optional Change Management Program.
You have noted that registration with HSA does not replace the hospital’s own testing in its own workflows.

sections.heading: Patient data
items: The data types that may be entered into the tool are specified, in line with the hospital’s data security classification.
The vendor says what it does with your data, whether it is used to train or improve its models, and where it is stored and processed.
Sub-processors, such as cloud and model providers, are named.
An exit plan covers the return or erasure of data when the contract ends.
Staff know what must never be typed into a generative AI tool.

sections.heading: Security and incidents
items: The vendor commits to telling you quickly about a data breach, and you know who answers at night.
You can shut the tool down and switch to a protocol that does not involve it.
Internal reporting routes exist for the PDPC (data), HSA (device adverse events) and the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (critical cybersecurity incidents).

sections.heading: Performance and fairness
items: The vendor can say on which patients the tool was tested and how they compare with yours.
The tool has been tested in your own workflows before go-live, with a pilot for higher-risk uses.
You know which performance figures will be monitored after go-live and who reports them.
For a tool that keeps learning, the vendor can show how it detects anomalies and rolls back.

sections.heading: Operations and people
items: A clinician makes the final decision wherever the output affects patient care.
Staff training is planned and covers limitations, output interpretation, data input restrictions and incident reporting.
The tool is entered in the hospital’s registry of AI solutions with its risk classification.
